# Preface {.unnumbered}

Bass players often know more than they can easily explain. A line can
live under the fingers for years before its internal logic becomes
explicit. This book is written for that gap. It assumes musical
intelligence but never assumes that technical facility guarantees a
complete mental model.

Our recurring loop is **HEAR -> NAME THE ROLE -> HEAR THE MOTION -> FEEL
THE GROOVE -> PLAY -> VARY -> COMPOSE**. Every chapter isolates one term
from `docs/vocabulary.md` so the ear can attribute what changed to the
concept that produced it.

## Why Role, Motion, and Groove instead of scales

This book deliberately avoids answering "which scale should I play?" or
"which arpeggio should I learn?" as its organizing question.

A scale or an arpeggio describes available pitches. It does not describe
what a bass line is *for* in a given moment — whether it is grounding
the harmony, redirecting it, or simply making the time feel good. Two
bass lines can share identical pitches and function completely
differently depending on their Role, their harmonic Motion, and their
Groove.

We therefore organize the entire book around three questions asked of
every example:

**What Role is this note playing? What Motion is it creating? What
Groove is it creating?**

Naming a scale answers none of these questions on its own. A concept
from this book's vocabulary always does.

## A note on notation

Every worked example pairs standard notation with a bass tab and with
inline Role/Motion/Groove annotations — see `docs/notation-conventions.md`
for the exact convention. The annotations are scaffolding: they exist so
you can see which decision produced which sound, and may be ignored once
that connection is audible without them.

No fingerings or right-hand/left-hand technique are prescribed; this
book is about what to play and why, not how to physically execute it on
a given instrument.

In this web edition, every notated example is also playable: press the
**Play** button beneath a score to hear it rendered at a plain, even
tempo. The audio is a plain synthesized reference, not a performance —
it exists so you can check what you think you're hearing against what
is actually on the page.

## Why we stay on one groove for so long

A method about relationships can paradoxically become harder to learn if
every example changes tempo, feel, and harmony at once. Many chapters
therefore return to a small set of fixed laboratory progressions so the
ear receives repeated exposure to the same harmonic and rhythmic ground
while only the chapter's own variable changes. Later chapters
deliberately vary the ground, once the relationship being taught is
stable enough to survive the change.

## The learning sequence

Every practical concept in this book follows the same order:

**hear the term in context -> isolate it in a short worked example ->
play it slowly against a click -> vary it once -> combine it with
already-known terms -> use it in an original bass line**

The order matters. Combining terms too early can hide the sound we are
trying to isolate. A concept should first become audible on its own.
Only then do we let it interact with everything the reader already
knows.

## How notation and practice work together

Exercises appear inside the relevant chapters so that sound and
explanation remain adjacent. The standalone `examples/` ABC repository
collects the same material for uninterrupted practice at the instrument.
